BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Increasing southwesterly flow on Thursday will allow for another few degrees of warmup, with dry conditions as brief shortwave ridging builds in ahead of the next system.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Light rain and mountain snow this afternoon through Tuesday morning, mainly in northern areas.
- Windy this afternoon in open southern areas.
- Continuing chance of light rain and snow showers in northern areas through Wednesday.
- Next best chance of widespread precipitation this weekend.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The upper-level low which will act as our next weather maker can be seen on water vapor imagery spinning off the Washington coast. With a cold front making its way through Oregon. This front should make it into our western zones before noon before moving across the area from west to east. Breezy south to southwest winds will set in this morning ahead of the front, with gusts to 20-30 mph. Behind the front, winds will become southwest to northwest. The windiest areas will generally be south and west of the Snake River Plain, and in the typical windy portions of the Snake River Plain. Winds will decrease behind the front this evening and overnight. Showers will increase along and behind the front as it moves from west to east, with coverage most widespread in the Central Idaho Mountains. While temperatures will be cool, cooling aloft as the upper low moves inland will support for weak instability to build in over the Central Idaho Mountains, supporting a slight chance (15-20%) of thunderstorms this afternoon. Following the passage of the front and upper-low, a trailing shortwave will prolong showers over our northern zones through Wednesday.

Over the course of today through Tuesday, higher terrain in our northern zones are forecast to receive generally 0.20-0.40 inches of liquid, with 0.10-0.20 in northern valleys and higher terrain south; elsewhere will be under 0.10 inches or dry. Lowering snow-levels behind the front will make for a transition to snow showers for elevations above 6kft MSL, with accumulations ranging from a dusting to around 2 inches (up to 4-5 inches on the highest peaks above 8kft MSL). Tuesday will be the coolest day of the short-term period, with lower elevation temps in the 50s and mountain valleys in the 40s (roughly 5 degrees cooler than today). Clearing Skies will allow for slightly cooler overnight lows Wednesday morning and slightly warmer daytime highs Wednesday afternoon, but seasonable temperatures for the time of year.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Increasing southwesterly flow on Thursday will allow for another few degrees of warmup, with dry conditions as brief shortwave ridging builds in ahead of the next system. Guidance seems to be backing off of the southern split solution mentioned in last nights discussion (if you read that one :) ), with ensembles now favoring a more northern track. With this, the best chances of precipitation will come over the weekend in southwest Idaho, after increasing late Friday in the Central Idaho Mountains. Snow levels for this system will range from 4-6kft MSL, increasing from west to east. Temperatures will continue to be seasonable for the time of year through the period.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: High uncertainty remains in the forecast Friday and into the weekend. A weak upper level shortwave will track across the southwestern United States and into the Central United States.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Areas of fog across the plains tonight through Tuesday morning.
- Warming trend and mostly dry for much of upcoming week.
- Unsettled weather potentially returning next weekend, but odds favor western and southern Colorado once again.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: A couple of quick updates this morning. First, it's pretty clear this wave is going to give many in the Denver metro more rain than originally promised. Despite an absence of any real upslope flow on the KFTG VAD, we've seen precipitation blossom across the Denver metro and Palmer Divide since midnight. There's been a few public gauges that have already received 0.25" or so since midnight across the far southwestern metro, perhaps enhanced a bit by the northerly surface flow. Most of the precipitation is tied to the strong vort max pivoting almost directly over the area this morning, which guidance has struggled to handle. We bumped up PoPs/QPF quite a bit in the near term to account for this. It wouldn't be surprising to see a couple half inch rainfall totals by the time most folks wake up later this morning.

Given the changes in the precipitation and low level moisture fields, it's also likely that stratus will be slower to erode than previously thought. We lowered high temperatures this afternoon by around 5 degrees to account for this, though some recent guidance (e.g., 06z HRRR) barely manages to get anyone into the 50s this afternoon. With the cooler/wetter trend for today, that also leads to a potentially foggy scenario for tonight into Tuesday morning. Will let the day shift take a full look at this but it wouldn't be surprising if we ended up with some dense fog across the northern metro and I-76 corridor.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Current radar imagery shows ongoing light showers across the forecast area as the upper level shortwave tracks across Colorado/Wyoming tonight. Mountain snow and rain showers over the plains will continue through tonight before exiting the region by Monday morning (most precip in Denver should be finished by sunrise, with the northeastern plains still seeing showers in the early morning). In terms of snowfall amounts across the high terrain, forecast looks to remain on track, with the northern mountains receiving generally 1-4" of snow by Monday morning and I-70 Corridor and south receiving T-2". Expect travel impacts across high mountain passes for the morning commute.

With low-level moisture still in place, many people will wake up to fog/low clouds in the morning across the Denver metro and plains, with possible impacts to morning commute due to low visibility. However, expect conditions to gradually improve by 9-10 AM with clearing skies in the afternoon. After that, an overall drying trend is expected as the upper level shortwave exits the region. We will still be relatively cool on Monday, given the slow morning warm-up, with highs in the upper 50s to low 60s.

Relatively dry and quiet conditions are expected for the forecast area Tuesday and through the end of the week, as more zonal flow aloft returns. An upper level low in the Pacific Northwest is progged to travel east across Idaho and Montana early this week. While it will stay north of Colorado, it will bring increased westerly flow aloft, resulting in breezy conditions across the high terrain Tuesday. Short-range models have been hinting at winds gusting up to 40-50 mph periodically in the morning. In terms of temperatures for the week, ensemble solutions are in good agreement of above-normal temperatures, with highs in the mid-to-high 60s across the plains.

High uncertainty remains in the forecast Friday and into the weekend. A weak upper level shortwave will track across the southwestern United States and into the Central United States. However, recent global model runs continue to hint that this disturbance will likely be too far south and east to impact our forecast area. For now, NBM PoPs of 10-20% seem reasonable at this time for the eastern plains on Friday, but wouldn't be surprised if it continues to lower in the coming days. After that, models vary drastically in handling the next upper level low that pushes through by the weekend/ early next week. CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Deterministic models are in better agreement for next weekend, but ensembles still depict relatively low confidence with precipitation chances...mainly due to the evolution and speed of the Pacific energy moving onshore.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Widespread rain showers and mountain snowfall expected through Monday morning as a central Pacific system lifts northeast across the region.
- Near normal temperatures and a bit warmer by Tuesday through Thursday, but the next Pacific system will be approaching from the eastern Pacific later in the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Much welcomed rainfall is ongoing across SE Wyoming and the Nebraska Panhandle at this hour associated an amplified open wave and a region of diffluence aloft. Latest MRMS QPE has estimated as much as 0.60" of rainfall has fallen across portions of Carbon and Albany Counties, with totals closer to 0.20" in Cheyenne. Amounts have been much lighter across the Panhandle at this time, which is expected to ramp up overnight into Monday morning as the shortwave trough lifts to the north and east.

Current surface observations show ENE upslope flow east of the Laramie Range, with temperatures mainly in the upper 30s to low 40s under low cloud cover, likely keeping our temperatures well above freezing through the overnight period. Radar imagery has shown quite a bit of bright banding this evening and overnight (ring of enhanced reflectivity collocated with reduced correlation coefficient), meaning that the melting layer isn't terribly far above the surface, so wouldn't be surprised to see some melting flakes mixed in with some of the heavier showers primarily across northern regions of the Panhandle, although no snow accumulation is expected. 00Z analysis combined with latest model guidance shows the main axis of isentropic ascent/warm advection gradually shifting more to the east over our Nebraska Panhandle counties towards sunrise, therefore expect precipitation coverage to increase through the night. Latest SPC Mesoanalysis shows a narrow region of 100-250 J/Kg of MUCAPE draped along the I-80 corridor across Kimball and Cheyenne Counties, so cannot rule out a lightning strike or two with some weak, embedded elevated convection, however decided to keep thunder out of the grids due to < 15% confidence and low coverage. High resolution ensemble guidance has median QPF ranging from 0.30" across the NW Panhandle, to as high as 0.75" further south and east, with lighter amounts across SE Wyoming in addition to what we have currently received. This seems reasonable given PWAT at the 99th percentile for this time of year, as we have a lot of total column moisture to work with. While certainly not a drought-buster, this is excellent moisture for drought-stricken areas as the current drought monitor has our region ranging anywhere from moderate (D1) to exceptional drought (D4). Expect precipitation coverage to gradually decrease from west to east as we head into the daytime on Monday morning, with SE Wyoming likely being dry come mid morning, and regions of the Nebraska Panhandle seeing precipitation exit the area by early afternoon. Low cloud cover may be stubborn tomorrow given the upslope flow regime, so high temperatures are expected to remain mainly in the 40s east of the Laramie Range, and low 50s to the west where fewer clouds are expected. One exception will be across the northern Panhandle where clouds and precipitation will stick around the longest, and ENE upslope flow will keep clouds banked up against the Pine Ridge.

Into Monday night, mostly dry conditions will prevail as this system exits our region and weak mid-level shortwave ridging builds in. Under the subsident flow and light winds, cannot rule out some low clouds east of the I-25 corridor given the damp soils, light winds, and residual moisture. Will let the day shift evaluate the potential for fog coverage Monday night into Tuesday morning as confidence remains too low at this time.

Tuesday will begin our warming trend as the flow regime becomes more WSW ahead of a trough located over the Pacific Northwest. As the ridge builds to our east, expect much milder day with high temperatures expected to reach the low 60s east of the I-25 corridor, with low to mid 50s to the west of the Laramie Range. Dry conditions are expected into Tuesday with temperatures largely remaining above freezing. Effective radiative cooling during the overnight period will be limited as 700 mb cross-barrier flow ramps up to 40-50 knots, which will increase our wind speeds at the surface into Tuesday morning.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Medium Range models remain in good agreement for much of mid to late week as weak to moderate southwest flow aloft dominates the weather pattern across the northern Front Range. With a lack of Pacific (shortwave) energy embedded in the mean southwest flow aloft through Friday, expect generally dry conditions and mild temperatures Wednesday through Friday as the polar jet stream will remain well to the north, and the subtropical jet should stay well south of the region near the Mexico/USA border and into Texas. Since southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska will be in between storm tracks, relatively mild temperatures are expected through the end of the week with afternoon highs in the upper 50s to upper 60s. Temperatures should peak Friday afternoon as 700mb temperatures climb over 5c ahead of the next Pacific storm system moving onshore, with a few locations possibly reaching 70 degrees east of the Interstate 25 corridor.

Deterministic models are in better agreement for next weekend, but ensembles still depict relatively low confidence with precipitation chances...mainly due to the evolution and speed of the Pacific energy moving onshore. Thankfully, with the Pacific energy trending a little slower, Halloween evening looks decent with maybe a few rain showers in the evening. Temperatures should be relatively mild for this time of the year in the upper 30s to upper 40s between sunset and 10:00 PM. Winds appear light and variable and should result in a pleasant evening. Models do show the first of a series of upper level disturbances lifting northward across the area on Halloween, but the system is pretty progressive with the best dynamics located north and west of the I-25 corridor. A more potent system is forecast to arrive on Sunday and continue early next week. Model solutions and ensemble members diverge significantly with this storm system, so will not go into too much detail at this time. However, temperatures will trend cooler and likely below average for this time of the year by next Sunday and Monday.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Southwest flow will begin to advect some moisture off the Pacific late Thursday into Friday, resulting in increased cloud cover.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Flooding and high flows along the San Juan river is ongoing across portions of southeast Utah, and is expected to continue through late Monday.
- Mountain passes could see minor snowfall amounts on roadways by Monday morning as this storm system exits to the northeast.
- Monday through Thursday is expected to be mostly dry, but another impactful system is possible next weekend.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Showers have become more isolated this evening as the low pressure system lifts northeast across northwest Colorado and exits to the northeast. Hi-res CAMs indicate most activity winding down by midnight and moving onto the Front Range east of the Divide by Monday morning. We could however still see some lingering orographic showers over the northern and central Divide Monday morning with light snow. Very little snow accumulation is expected but conditions could be slick in the morning over the passes.

Much drier air moves in Monday and lasts through at least mid week as a shortwave high pressure ridge slides overhead Monday. A couple shortwave troughs will push across the Intermountain West from the PacNW Monday night through Tuesday night, resulting in a breezy southwest flow Tuesday afternoon and some light showers possible over the northern mountains. Overall conditions remain dry with little in the way of precipitation through mid week as temperatures hover around 5 degrees below normal with a warmup towards normal or slightly above by Thursday.

Southwest flow will begin to advect some moisture off the Pacific late Thursday into Friday, resulting in increased cloud cover. Models are not in the best agreement beyond Friday with regards to how to handle this influx of Pacific moisture but showers are possible Friday afternoon, particularly over the southern and central Divide as a shortwave trough skirts the Front Range from the southwest. A deeper trough moves into the west Sunday into early next week but the jury is out on what this means for our weather. While conditions look to turn more unsettled with increasing moisture from the Pacific, there are discrepancies between models and model runs on timing, how cold it might get, and the duration of said moisture as some of the latest model runs are showing a more progressive solution than earlier runs. This is still a ways out but due to poor model agreement and poor model consistency, will hold off on discussing too much detail yet. This is the next system to watch, which could result in a return to cooler and unsettled conditions with potential for mountain snowfall.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Our next pattern change will arrive around this weekend. A broad upper trough and associated low pressure system will amplify over the Pacific Northwest, digging south and moving onshore by Saturday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Drier and warmer starting today, lasting through most of the week.
- Pattern change arrives this weekend, bringing cooler and more active weather to the region again.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Any lingering showers out east will dissipate by late morning, giving way to warmer and drier conditions across the region. High temperatures for today will be in the 60s out east, with 50s over the valleys. Cloud cover will decrease substantially, with relatively light winds. Overall, a warm and mild fall day. That being said, ongoing high flows across the Rio Grande and Conejos Rivers will continue for at least another few days. Conditions should be closely monitored for ongoing impacts.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Warm and dry through the rest of the week. Temperatures will continue to reach into the high-60s to low-70s each day over the plains and 50s in the valleys, with generally mild weather across the region.

Our next pattern change will arrive around this weekend. A broad upper trough and associated low pressure system will amplify over the Pacific Northwest, digging south and moving onshore by Saturday. Flow aloft over our area will turn southwesterly, bringing in more moisture to the mountains, and then possibly the rest of the CWA as well. There still is a lot of deviation between model solutions, so time will tell how impactful the system will actually be for our area. We should see a decent chance at some more widespread precipitation, and hopefully more snow for the mountains.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Thereafter, models are still pointing to an active pattern for the weekend into potentially early next week as a strengthening storm system over the PacNW phases with a second system originating farther west that taps into a plume of moisture.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A couple of weak storm systems will bring generally light valley rain and mountain snow to northern Utah Monday night and Tuesday night.
- A more substantial storm arrives by the end of the week into the weekend with the potential for widespread precipitation that could increase the risk of flash flooding.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The upper low that has brought showers to the area the last couple of days is now centered over southwest Wyoming as it continues to exit the area. Behind this low, showers have mostly dissipated over Utah this evening. A transient shortwave ridge will cross the area late tonight through Monday morning before southwesterly flow aloft increases ahead of the next trough which is currently noted over the PacNW coast. Fairly benign weather can be expected into early Monday evening. Temperatures on Monday will trend warmer, rising to near to slightly above normal across northern Utah but remaining below normal across the south.

The upstream trough will end up grazing northern Utah late Monday evening through Monday night. This will push a relatively shallow cold front into northern Utah. A quick round of showers is expected to accompany this front. The latest high-res models are not as enthusiastic about precipitation compared to the global models. For example, the 75th percentile of the REFS is only showing 0.15-0.3 inches in the Bear River Range, with generally less than 0.1 inches in the adjacent valleys and no measurable precipitation south of around Ogden. Meanwhile, the NBM 50th percentile has slightly higher amounts than that. Suspect the NBM will trend downward with the global deterministics trending towards a weaker cold front. With snow levels falling as low as 6500 feet near the Idaho border, some light snow accumulations can be expected over the higher terrain.

Cooler temperatures can be expected again on Tuesday behind the cold front, with northern Utah trending back to slightly below normal temperatures. Otherwise, any precipitation from the cold front will clear the area by around sunrise, leading to mostly clear skies during the morning through late afternoon. Southwesterly flow aloft will quickly redevelop as a second, weakening trough swings into the northern Great Basin. This trough will then eject across northern Utah Tuesday night, bringing another potential round of light precipitation to northern Utah. Deterministic models have this second trough trending slightly stronger, which falls in line with the first trough trending slightly weaker.

Thereafter, models are still pointing to an active pattern for the weekend into potentially early next week as a strengthening storm system over the PacNW phases with a second system originating farther west that taps into a plume of moisture. Latest global deterministics are introducing greater timing uncertainties in that the 18z GFS does not bring any precipitation into Utah until Saturday evening, compared to earlier runs and the EC which have precipitation beginning as early as Friday. Nevertheless, Sunday looks to be the wettest day at this time. However, there remains some model spread regarding how the large-scale pattern evolves through the weekend and how quickly the storm exits the area.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Heavy rain on Wednesday and Thursday triggered small wet avalanches in the west-Central and Southern Mountains, but this concern is waning as temperatures drop. The most likely place to trigger an avalanche is at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) in the Southern and west-Central Mountains on west, north, and east-facing slopes where new snow has been accumulating and a layer of mid-October snow persists. The Northern Mountains remain mostly bare.

This weekend, a new storm will deliver 4 to 8 inches of snow to the San Juan and Sangre de Cristo Mountains, creating fresh avalanche concerns on upper-elevation, wind-drifted slopes facing west, north, and east. Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
